sources.title: Dummies
sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health
sources.quote: Give your child the chance to stop their dummy habit when they are ready. Most children stop sucking habits between the ages of two and four, but you can start the process from around one year of age. ... Avoid trying to stop dummy use suddenly, as it can lead to other oral habits such as thumb or finger sucking. ... Limit the use of the dummy to sleep or nighttime. ... Talk about stopping the dummy for a couple of days to prepare your child. ... Consider replacing it with a toy, maybe a cuddly toy they have chosen and can hold when they would be using the dummy. You can talk about the replacement when they are asking for the dummy. ... Persist gently but firmly. The first few days without a dummy are likely to be the most difficult.
sources.supports: Stopping gradually, limiting the dummy to sleep, preparing the child by talking for a couple of days, a chosen cuddly toy in its place and that the first few days are the hardest. An Australian state health service page, applied to Israeli families as general child health advice.

sources.title: Weaning off dummies and bottles
sources.publisher: Sheffield Children's NHS Foundation Trust, Resource Library
sources.quote: Start by just letting your child use their dummy for nap times and bed time. Try to swap it out for their favourite toy or teddy to hold onto for comfort instead. ... Once they are using their dummy less, set a date for being ‘dummy free’. Help them by giving them lots of praise, and give them lots of positive attention. ... Make sure you and other caregivers remove any bottles and dummies from your child’s sight. ... Try creating some fun around leaving the dummy behind. For example use a ‘Dummy Fairy’ that takes it away during the night and leaves a small reward. Remember that this can be a difficult and challenging time for them.
sources.supports: Dummy only for naps and bedtime first, a favourite toy for comfort, a dummy free date once use is down, praise, keeping it out of sight and making the goodbye fun (a Dummy Fairy). An NHS trust leaflet for UK families, used as general advice.

sources.title: Dummies
sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health
sources.quote: Give your child the chance to stop their dummy habit when they are ready. Most children stop sucking habits between the ages of two and four, but you can start the process from around one year of age. ... Avoid trying to stop dummy use suddenly, as it can lead to other oral habits such as thumb or finger sucking. ... Limit the use of the dummy to sleep or nighttime. ... Talk about stopping the dummy for a couple of days to prepare your child. ... Consider replacing it with a toy, maybe a cuddly toy they have chosen and can hold when they would be using the dummy. You can talk about the replacement when they are asking for the dummy. ... Persist gently but firmly. The first few days without a dummy are likely to be the most difficult.
sources.supports: Stopping gradually, limiting the dummy to sleep, preparing the child by talking for a couple of days, a chosen cuddly toy in its place and that the first few days are the hardest. An Australian state health service page, applied to Israeli families as general child health advice.

sources.title: Weaning off dummies and bottles
sources.publisher: Sheffield Children's NHS Foundation Trust, Resource Library
sources.quote: Start by just letting your child use their dummy for nap times and bed time. Try to swap it out for their favourite toy or teddy to hold onto for comfort instead. ... Once they are using their dummy less, set a date for being ‘dummy free’. Help them by giving them lots of praise, and give them lots of positive attention. ... Make sure you and other caregivers remove any bottles and dummies from your child’s sight. ... Try creating some fun around leaving the dummy behind. For example use a ‘Dummy Fairy’ that takes it away during the night and leaves a small reward. Remember that this can be a difficult and challenging time for them.
sources.supports: Dummy only for naps and bedtime first, a favourite toy for comfort, a dummy free date once use is down, praise, keeping it out of sight and making the goodbye fun (a Dummy Fairy). An NHS trust leaflet for UK families, used as general advice.

sources.publisher: Child Mind Institute (last reviewed 6 Nov 2023)
sources.quote: Instead, emphasize that you hear your child and express your support for how they're handling this. ... Working with your child to plan out their days is one way to give them a sense of control over what's happening. ... sources.supports: Hear and support the child's feeling instead of dismissing it, do not judge the reaction, plan the day together for a sense of control, and point out the skills the child already has. A general page about disappointment, applied to a birthday that does not go to plan.

post_text.caption:
בדמיון יום מושלם ובאמת העוגה נשברת, תעזרו לי. 🎉
תגידו לי שיכול להשתבש ותחשבו איתי מה אם.
תנו לי לתת רעיונות ותראו לי איך מסתדרים.
תדברו איתי לפני שמתחילים ותנו לי לבחור חלק.
ובערב אפשר להמשיך עם סיפור שבו אני הגיבור.
תשמרו את הפוסט לפעם הבאה שיש לו יום הולדת 🔖
post_text.fb_text:
כל כך חיכיתי לו 🎉
שקשה לי כשהוא שונה,
אני לא עושה דווקא,
אני פשוט מאוכזב.

1 תגידו שיכול להשתבש,
ושזה בסדר,
גם ביום הולדת.

2 נחשוב ביחד מה אם,
״אם הגשם ירד מה נעשה?״,
בלי להבטיח, רק לחשוב.

3 תנו לי לתת רעיונות,
אני אומר מה אפשר לעשות,
אם משהו לא יוצא.

4 תראו לי איך מסתדרים,
אם משהו משתבש תגידו,
״בואו נמצא פתרון״

5 נדבר לפני שמתחילים,
6 תגידו מה מצפים ממני,
מה אני אמור לעשות,
כשהאורחים מגיעים.

7 תנו לי לבחור חלק,
8 תפרגנו לי אחר כך,
אני בוחר שיר או משחק,
״ליאור ראיתי איך חזרת לעצמך״

נחשוב ביחד לפני,
ואז קל לי יותר,
גם אם משהו ישתבש,
תהיו לידי ונמצא פתרון.

תשמרו את הפוסט,
לפעם הבאה,
שיש לו יום הולדת 🔖
